title: To the tune of a king's ballad
word: To the tune of a king's ballad
hook: the heading says it's sung to the tune of a folk ballad about a king, and ragis sing it with chhants between

segments.voice: Yesterday, var, and your line: the dawn ballad. Did the first minute of your morning go to something worth singing to? Today, before a single pauri, we read the small print at the top of Asa di Var. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

Plenty of hymns borrowed their tunes from somewhere else. A melody from a tavern, a folk song everybody's grandmother knew, a march from a parade ground: give it new words and suddenly a whole room can sing along, because they already know how it goes. The trick is old, and it's everywhere. Above the first line of Asa di Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's a heading. Most people skip right past it. It tells you exactly which old tune to use.
screen: `A HYMN ON A BORROWED TUNE.` → `EVERYONE ALREADY KNOWS HOW IT GOES.` → `THE HEADING ABOVE ASA DI VAR.`

segments.voice: The heading says, in paraphrase: Asa, the first Guru. A var, with saloks, and saloks also written by the first Guru, to be sung to the tune of Tunda Asraj. Dhunee is the word for tune. And Tunda Asraj was the subject of a folk ballad people in Punjab knew: Asraj, a king, often described as tunda, maimed or one-handed. The story behind the ballad is told in more than one version, usually about a prince who's wronged and wounded but rises to rule. The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't retell it. It just names the tune, and expects the singer to know how it goes. That's the striking thing. Guru Nanak didn't invent a sacred melody that only the trained could sing. He reached for a folk tune ordinary people already carried in their heads, and gave it new words: words about God as the true King, and about the inner battle. Several other vars in the Guru Granth Sahib carry similar headings, naming the folk tunes they were meant to follow. Then there's how it's sung today. Ragis usually pair Asa di Var with the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, also in raag Asa. A chhant is sung, then a pauri with its saloks, then the next chhant, so the fourth Guru's verses and the first Guru's ballad take turns. Three Gurus' voices, braided together, every morning. Old tunes, new words, and many hands in the weaving.
screen: `THE HEADING: TUNDA ASRAJ'S TUNE.` · `DHUNEE: A TUNE PEOPLE KNEW.` · `A FOLK TUNE, NEW WORDS.` · `CHHANTS AND PAURIS TAKE TURNS.` · then, large: `OLD TUNES, NEW WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum any old tune. Pick a melody you've known for years: a lullaby, a song from childhood, something your family sang in the car. Hum it softly, slowly. Notice how your body already knows it, how the next note arrives before you think. Then let the humming fade, and sit with the quiet it leaves. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride on the tune as you hum. The bell holds the time.
To the tune of a king's ballad. Asa di Var's heading names the folk tune of Tunda Asraj: an old melody, given new words about God.
screen: `TO THE TUNE OF A KING'S BALLAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: old tunes, new words. Today, take one old habit, a walk, a commute, a chore, and give it a new purpose, like a borrowed tune. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 537 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

original.note: Gurmukhi: dhunee, tune or melody; the heading names the dhunee of Tunda Asraj.

trapdoor: what you thought: the heading is just a title.
what it means: it tells the singer which folk tune to use, the ballad of Tunda Asraj, so anyone could sing along.

notes: Heading paraphrase (aasaa mahalaa 1, vaar salokaa naal salok bhee mahale pahile ke likhe, tunde as-raajai kee dhunee): confirm wording.
The Asraj legend varies; the script says only that he was a king described as tunda and the story is told in more than one version.
Who added the dhunee headings (often attributed to Guru Arjan) is left unstated; a Keeper may add it. Ang range for Guru Ram Das's Asa chhants (448–451) is approximate: confirm.
